title: The storm (Luke 8:22–25)
hookLine: the boat is swamping, Jesus is asleep, and the disciples shout him awake

cards: Three in the morning, when a worry gets loud: the bill, the diagnosis, the text you shouldn't have sent. Everything is going under, and everyone else seems asleep. Now a fishing boat on the Sea of Galilee.
Jesus says, let's go over to the other side, and they push off. The lake sits low among hills, and storms can drop onto it fast. As they sail, Luke says, Jesus falls asleep.
Then the wind comes down, the waves come over the side, and the boat fills with water. These are fishermen who know this lake, and they're terrified.

teach.b: They wake him with a shout, in the King James Bible: "Master, master, we perish." Mark's telling is rawer: "Master, carest thou not that we perish?" Don't you care?
It's one of the most honest prayers in the Bible, shouted at a sleeping man in a sinking boat, and the text doesn't scold them for it.
Then Luke says: "he arose, and rebuked the wind and the raging of the water: and they ceased, and there was a calm." Mark gives his words to the sea: "Peace, be still."
He talks to the storm the way you'd calm a frightened animal. Then comes a silence so big it frightens them in a new way; Mark says they feared exceedingly. He asks: "Where is your faith?"

teach.h: WHAT MANNER OF MAN IS THIS?
teach.b: And they whisper to each other: "What manner of man is this! for he commandeth even the winds and water, and they obey him." In the Hebrew scriptures, the one who stills the sea is God.
One psalm says of sailors in a storm: "He maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still." That's the question the story leaves in the boat: who is this?

teach.h: THE NAVE: THE CHURCH AS A BOAT.
teach.b: Christians have long seen the church as a boat on rough water, and the main hall of many church buildings is still called the nave, from the Latin for ship.
One more thing: he was in the boat the whole time. Asleep, but there. The story doesn't promise there'll be no storms.
It puts him in the same wet boat as everyone else.

how: Many Christians turn to this story in times of fear and illness, and it's often read at services for people at sea. The image of the church as a ship shows up in church architecture, in hymns, and in the name nave for the main hall.

o: a sudden gale that nearly sank the disciples' boat
a flood that covered the earth in Noah's day
God's punishment sent on a runaway prophet

games.q: who said what — tap the pairs.
p: carest thou not that we perish?

s: Jesus was awake and praying when the storm hit
Luke says he fell asleep as they sailed, and they had to wake him.
the church's main hall, the nave, is named from the Latin for ship
the church has long been pictured as a boat on rough water.
the disciples were calm once the storm stopped
they were afraid and amazed: what manner of man is this?

games.q: you're in the boat. the waves are coming over the side, it's filling with water, and your teacher is asleep. what do you do?
o: bail quietly and let him sleep.
shout him awake: master, we perish!
games.why: they wake him with a shout. he rebukes the wind and the water, and there's a great calm. the text never scolds them for shouting.

practice: Feel your feet on the floor and name the storm you're in, the specific one that keeps you up, quietly out loud in one sentence, plain, the way the disciples said it.
Then take three slow breaths, letting your shoulders drop on each out-breath. If you pray, you can shout it honestly, as they did, or say Peace, be still; if you don't, let the breath be the calm.

wordCard.voice: The storm. A swamping boat, a sleeping teacher, a shout of don't you care, and a calm that frightened them all over again.

orig.note: Greek, from Mark: be silent, be muzzled. The words the KJV renders peace, be still.

carryVoice: Your line: peace, be still. Three words to a storm, and then a calm. That's day fifty-five.
